<strong>Es gibt daher keine empirisch ab: There is therefore no empirically grounded distribution of the muslim population across districts or municipalities. Anteil der 18- bis 29-Jährigen an den Ei: Share of 18- to 29-year-olds among the inhabitants of the cell. The map largely traces the university towns — Heidelberg, Tübingen, Freiburg, Konstanz — and alongside them the inner-city districts of the larger cities. It works as a counter-image to the foreign-national layer: where both are high there is usually a university, and that is something other than an immigrant district. Anteil der Bevölkerung ohne deutsche Sta: Share of the population without German citizenship per government region (NUTS 2), added up from the district figures. Naturalised persons and descendants born here hold a German passport and do not appear in these figures.

Share of the population without German citizenship, reference date 31 December 2025. The same measure as the 2024 layer, one year later and updated by the federal government instead of the state. The difference is small: the median across districts is 17.2 percent in both years, and the largest deviation for any district is 0.4 percentage points. Both layers stand side by side so this can be checked rather than simply asserted.
Share of the population without German citizenship. Calculated in-house from concurrent official register data. No indication of religion, country of birth, or parents' origin.
Anteil der Einwohnerinnen und Einwohner: Share of residents without German citizenship, by municipality. Naturalised persons and their children born in Germany count as Germans and are invisible here — in long-established communities that is the majority. A municipality with a low share of foreign nationals can still have a long-established immigrant population. This is measured, not modelled: the only directly recorded figure the atlas can place alongside the model calculation at municipality level.
Anteil der Erwerbspersonen — erwerbstäti: Share of the labour force — in work, or unemployed and looking — among the foreign-born aged 20 to 64. The difference from the unemployment rate is the whole point: someone who neither works nor looks for work appears in no unemployment rate. Two regions with the same unemployment rate can therefore look very different, and the gap to the native-born is shown in the profile.

Share of the labour force — employed or unemployed and seeking — among the foreign-born aged 20 to 64. People neither working nor seeking do not count; that is what distinguishes this measure from the unemployment rate. Seven of the nine measures come from the Labour Force Survey, that is from a sample. For small regions the uncertainty is correspondingly larger; Eurostat does not report it per region. Not samples are the net migration rate, which comes from population projection, and the arrival rate from the 2021 Census.
Anteil der Erwerbstätigen an der Bevölke: Share of employed persons among the population aged 15 and over with a migration background. Sample survey. No unemployment rate, because the source withholds the number of unemployed persons for almost all districts for confidentiality. These figures do not feed into any model calculation in this atlas.
Anteil der Menschen mit türkischer Staat: Share of people with Turkish citizenship among the inhabitants of the cell. Three things this map does NOT show. First, no religion: Turkish citizenship is not a religious affiliation, and the census records none. Second, not people of Turkish origin: most of them hold a German passport in Baden-Württemberg and are absent here entirely — what the map shows is the smaller, non-naturalised part. Third, no completeness: only 6,581 of the 21,585 inhabited cells carry a value, and an empty cell means either nobody or too few to be allowed to say. Shares are formed only from 30 inhabitants per cell upwards, because secrecy shifts small numbers by exactly the order of magnitude at stake.
Anteil der Menschen ohne deutschen Pass: Share of people without a German passport per grid cell of one kilometre. A municipality like Stuttgart has a single value for 610,000 inhabitants on every other layer of this atlas; only here can you see how different its neighbourhoods are. Empty areas are two things at once and cannot be told apart: uninhabited, or kept secret. The census suppresses small cases and perturbs the rest using the cell-key method — of 21,585 inhabited cells only 13,516 carry a foreign-national share. Reading the gaps as empty land misreads the map.
Anteil der Mitglieder der evangelischen: Share of members of the Protestant church in the population, from the 2022 census. The mirror image of the layer beside it, and almost literally so: together the two maps show the confessional boundary of 1555, still visible in the settlement pattern today. 25.9 per cent statewide; both churches together 55.8 per cent.
Anteil der Mitglieder der römisch-kathol: Share of members of the Roman Catholic church in the population, from the 2022 census. This is the most pronounced religious structure Baden-Württemberg has: Catholic Upper Swabia and the south against Protestant old Württemberg. 29.9 per cent statewide. Counted, not estimated — unlike the Muslim population, for which no survey exists at municipal level. Individual values are protected by the cell-key method and are therefore deliberately slightly perturbed.
Anteil der Mitglieder evangelischer Frei: Share of members of Protestant free churches in the district population, 2011 Census — the second group the 2022 Census lets disappear into the residual category. 1.1 per cent statewide, a good 119,000 people. The layer is here because free churches come up repeatedly in this atlas’s surveys: in the KONID survey, respondents counted among them agree more often than any other group that their own religion takes precedence over the constitution in case of conflict. How large the group being talked about there is, this map says.
Anteil der Mitglieder orthodoxer Kirchen: Share of members of Orthodox churches in the district population, 2011 Census. This is the only count there is for them: the 2022 Census no longer reports the public-law religious societies separately but puts everything except the two large churches into one residual category. In 2011 Baden-Württemberg had the highest Orthodox population share of any state at 2.1 per cent, against 1.3 per cent nationally; the peak is Stuttgart at 5.3 per cent. Three limits belong to every one of these figures. What is counted is registered membership of a public-law corporation, not who considers themselves Orthodox — which church holds that status differs from church to church and from state to state, and the Syriac Orthodox Church, for instance, appears only where it has it. And the reference date is 9 May 2011: the arrivals from Romania, Bulgaria, Syria, Iraq and Ukraine came after it. The map is therefore a lower bound, not a present state. One category is missing here altogether: no Islamic community holds corporation status in Baden-Württemberg, so Muslims appear in the row „Member of no public-law religious society“ — together with everyone of no faith.
Anteil der Personen ohne Pass des Wohnsi: Share of people without the passport of their country of residence in the population aged 15 to 64 in private households. The same definition as elsewhere in this atlas. Seven of the nine measures come from the Labour Force Survey, that is from a sample. For small regions the uncertainty is correspondingly larger; Eurostat does not report it per region. Not samples are the net migration rate, which comes from population projection, and the arrival rate from the 2021 Census.

Share of people without a passport of the country they live in. This is the same definition used on the district and municipal layers of this atlas — unlike country of birth, naturalised citizens are not counted here. What is comparable is the definition, not the number: Eurostat counts only people aged 15 to 64 in private households, and because immigrants are over-represented in those age groups the value is higher than the share across all ages. For the Stuttgart region 25.3 instead of 19.8 per cent.
Anteil der ausländischen Bevölkerung des: Share of the district's foreign population holding Turkish citizenship. Not the number of people of Turkish origin: naturalised persons and their descendants born here hold a German passport and are entirely absent. Nationwide median: 7.5 percent.

Share of the district's foreign population originating from the guest-worker recruitment countries — Turkey, Italy, Greece, Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Tunisia, former Yugoslavia. The denominator is the district's foreign population, not its total population.

Share of the district's foreign population that has lived in Germany for at least 25 years. This figure, too, counts only people without a German passport — precisely among the long-established, naturalised persons are missing, so the length of stay of origin groups tends to be underestimated. Nationwide median: 17.4 percent.
Anteil der ausländischen Bevölkerung mit: Share of the foreign population resident for at least 25 years — the counterpart to the district layer of the same name, one level up. Baden-Württemberg ranks first of all states at 27.4 per cent: its foreign population is longer established than anywhere else. In the east the value lies between 4 and 7 per cent. This measure in particular understates length of residence, because those here longest are the most likely to have been naturalised and then leave the register.
Anteil der hier geborenen Menschen mit d: Share of people born here with a German passport among the population with a migration background. These are precisely the people missing from the foreign-national statistics — which is why the model calculation needs a correction for naturalised persons and descendants. No indication of religious affiliation.
Anteil der im Ausland Geborenen an der B: Share of the foreign-born in the population aged 15 to 64 in private households. What is counted is place of birth, not passport. Seven of the nine measures come from the Labour Force Survey, that is from a sample. For small regions the uncertainty is correspondingly larger; Eurostat does not report it per region. Not samples are the net migration rate, which comes from population projection, and the arrival rate from the 2021 Census.

Share of foreign-born people among the population aged 15 to 64 in private households. What is counted is the place of birth, not the passport: naturalised citizens are included here and are not included in the foreign-national share of the other layers. Labour Force Survey sample; correspondingly uncertain for small regions.
Anteil der in Deutschland Geborenen an d: Share of people born in Germany among the state’s foreign population. The usual objection to any passport-based figure is that those born here are missing — here it is quantified, as far as they hold no German passport. North Rhine-Westphalia leads with 15.0 per cent, Baden-Württemberg follows with 13.2; in the eastern states the value is 7 to 9 per cent because immigration there is more recent. Not included are naturalised people and children who become German at birth under section 4(3) of the Nationality Act.
Anteil der unter 25-Jährigen an der Bevö: Share of people under 25 among the population with a migration background. Hatched: the source withholds too many age groups to form a reliable share. Migration background is a far larger group than the modelled muslim population; this is not that group's age structure.

Share of people under 25 in the population, from the Zensus 2022. Unlike the district layer from the Mikrozensus, this is a full census and available for all municipalities. No indication of religious affiliation and not a variable in the model calculation.
Anteil der unter 25-Jährigen an der ausl: Share of people under 25 among the district's foreign population. Statewide this is 24.6 percent — 24.9 percent for the German population, so practically the same. This is partly an artefact of how the count works: children of immigrants who are naturalised or born German count on the German side and are missing on the foreign side. This is explicitly not a comparison of the age structure of origin groups.
Anteil derer, die 2010 oder später einge: Share of those who arrived in 2010 or later among the foreign-born whose year of arrival is known. A high value means recent immigration, a low one a long-established population — the counterpart to the district layer "resident for 25 years", except that there the passport counts and here the place of birth. From the 2021 census: a full count across all ages, not a sample estimate, but a single snapshot with no update. Cases with no year of arrival are left out of the denominator rather than quietly counted among the long-established; their share is shown in each region's profile. In 15 of the 251 regions — in Czechia, France and Slovakia — it is missing for more than a fifth, in Baden-Württemberg for at most a tenth.

Share of those who arrived in 2010 or later among the foreign-born with a known year of arrival. A high value means recent immigration, a low one a long-settled population. 2021 Census, all ages, a full count rather than a sample. Seven of the nine measures come from the Labour Force Survey, that is from a sample. For small regions the uncertainty is correspondingly larger; Eurostat does not report it per region. Not samples are the net migration rate, which comes from population projection, and the arrival rate from the 2021 Census.
Anteil mit tertiärem Abschluss (ISCED 5–: Share with tertiary education (ISCED 5–8) among the foreign-born aged 25 to 64 in private households. Seven of the nine measures come from the Labour Force Survey, that is from a sample. For small regions the uncertainty is correspondingly larger; Eurostat does not report it per region. Not samples are the net migration rate, which comes from population projection, and the arrival rate from the 2021 Census.
Anteil mit tertiärem Abschluss an den im: Share with a tertiary qualification among the foreign-born aged 25 to 64. This layer separates out one of the four things bundled into the employment rate gap. It also shows what an average conceals: in the Stuttgart region 28.7 per cent of the foreign-born hold a university degree and 35.0 per cent have at most lower secondary education — the group is strongly represented at both ends, not in the middle. Both figures and the gap to the native-born are in each region's profile.
